calculation.substitution: Safaricom: floor(KES 6,529.55 ÷ KES 36.65) = 178 shares.
calculation.interpretation: Source share cost KES 6,523.70; cost plus maximum modeled fees KES 6,660.70.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Price changes alter the affordable quantity
scenario.baseline: Keep the monthly allocation and fee budget fixed.
scenario.changed: Increase the observed share price before executing the order.
scenario.consequence: Recalculate whole shares and residual cash; do not force the original quantity through the cash limit.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: DCA — investing fixed contributions at scheduled dates
Whole shares — integer quantity affordable within cash limits
Residual cash — unspent amount after share purchases and costs
action: Save the purchase log with capital budget, source price date, fees, integer shares and review trigger.
case: A dated KES 100,000 teaching allocation staged through three monthly purchases with fees and whole-share constraints.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: A staged contribution plan must fit fees, whole-share quantities and residual cash. Dividend assessment then asks whether the underlying business can sustain the payment.

beats.title: A watchlist is a research queue
points: Record why each candidate could fill a portfolio role.
A candidate may remain deferred while evidence is missing.
A new ticker does not automatically add a new economic exposure.

Look through overlapping holdings before calling the portfolio diversified.

beats.title: Make entry discipline inspectable
points: Record the price date, valuation range and source.
Set required evidence and the condition that rules out a purchase.
Review quarterly and after a material change; expire stale theses.

calculation.title: Read the current core before adding a candidate
calculation.equation: Combined sector weight = sum of constituent position weights
calculation.substitution: Equity 15% + Co-operative Bank 15% + Standard Chartered Kenya 15% = 45%.
calculation.interpretation: Three separate holdings still leave 45% of the illustrative target in banks.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: The new bank candidate may deepen an existing tilt
scenario.baseline: The example core already targets 45% in three banks.
scenario.changed: Consider another bank without reducing existing bank holdings.
scenario.consequence: Sector exposure rises; compare its incremental role and risk before adding a position.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Target weight — desired proportion of the portfolio
Concentration — exposure clustered in related claims
Watchlist — research candidates with an evidence status
action: Add a candidate with source links, a valuation range, an exposure role and pass/revise/defer status.
case: An investor compares new research candidates with an existing Kenyan equity core, preserving the option to defer.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: A watchlist broadens research when each candidate has an evidence requirement and a portfolio role. A deferred decision can be the correct output.

beats.title: Start with the economic claim
points: A company operates a business; a security defines an investor claim.
An exchange is a trading venue, while an index is a rule-based measurement.
A fund holds assets under a mandate; a portfolio combines claims for a purpose.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Benchmarks answer different questions
points: A large-company benchmark differs from a broad market or growth-heavy benchmark.
Weighting rules affect whose returns dominate the result.
Compare total return, currency and time period on a consistent basis.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Risk has more than one dimension
points: Volatility measures variability, while a drawdown describes a peak-to-trough loss.
Liquidity affects whether an investor can transact at a useful price.
Match horizon, spending currency and acceptable loss before selecting a wrapper.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: A return changes a starting claim
calculation.equation: Ending value = beginning value × (1 + total return)
calculation.substitution: Teaching input: USD 10,000 × 1.08 = USD 10,800.
calculation.interpretation: An 8% illustrative total return says nothing by itself about the next period or the investor’s spending-currency return.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: A drawdown needs a larger percentage recovery
scenario.baseline: Teaching balance falls from USD 10,000 to USD 8,000: −20%.
scenario.changed: Recover from USD 8,000 to the original USD 10,000.
scenario.consequence: Required return is 10,000/8,000 − 1 = 25%, before withdrawals or costs.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Total return — price change plus distributions; stated reinvestment basis
Benchmark — rule-defined market measurement
Drawdown — loss from a prior peak; %
Liquidity — ability to transact at a usable price
action: Write purpose, spending currency, time horizon and acceptable loss before choosing a fund.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: The economic claim, benchmark and ownership vehicle answer different questions. Define the investor’s job for the money before combining them into a portfolio.

beats.title: A wrapper changes implementation
points: Direct shares, mutual funds and ETFs package ownership differently.
Creation and redemption connect ETF shares with the underlying basket.
Legal structure, dealing mechanics and investor eligibility belong in the comparison.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Count four layers of cost
points: The fund expense ratio compounds inside the investment.
Spread, commissions and market impact affect execution.
Tax, currency conversion and funding affect what the household retains.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Make the fee comparison comparable
points: Keep the gross return, horizon and contributions the same.
Date each published fee and benchmark description.
Different exposures cannot be ranked solely by expense ratio.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: A recurring fee compounds
calculation.equation: FV = P × (1 + r − e)ⁿ
calculation.substitution: USD 10,000 at 8% gross less 0.020% annual fee → USD 100,069.03 after 30 years.
calculation.interpretation: Under the same gross-return assumption, the source 0.750% fee case ends at USD 81,643.01.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Keep the exposure assumption; change only the fee
scenario.baseline: Source 30-year ending value at 0.020% fee: USD 100,069.03.
scenario.changed: Source active-fund illustration at 0.750% fee: USD 81,643.01.
scenario.consequence: Fee-only gap is USD 18,426.02. This holds gross returns equal and is not a performance forecast.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: P — initial principal; USD
r — assumed gross annual return; decimal
e — recurring annual expense ratio; decimal
n — investment horizon; years
FV — ending value before excluded tax/transaction costs; USD
action: Record eligible wrappers and the full cost path, including funding, execution, tax and exit.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: What the investor retains depends on recurring costs, execution, tax and funding together. A low stated fee helps only within an exposure and ownership structure that fits the investor.

beats.title: Begin with the investor’s facts
points: Record residence, citizenship, account owner and relevant treaty position.
Separate the legal domicile from the exchange and dealing currency.
Trace the dividend from company through fund to investor.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Separate withholding from estate exposure
points: A payment-tax assumption does not resolve an ownership-at-death question.
Retain account, security and beneficiary records.
Use dated rules and investor-specific eligibility before implementing a route.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Currency belongs in the same record
points: Fund denomination and trading currency do not define every underlying exposure.
Match near-term cash obligations to their spending currency.
Compare custody, funding, reporting and exit costs as one implementation path.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: Trace the withholding cash flow
calculation.equation: Net dividend = position × dividend yield × (1 − withholding rate)
calculation.interpretation: At an illustrative eligible 15% rate, net cash is USD 110.50: a USD 19.50 difference before other costs.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Treaty eligibility changes the payment assumption
scenario.baseline: No-treaty illustration: 30% withholding on USD 130.
scenario.changed: Eligible illustrative treaty treatment: 15% on the same USD 130.
scenario.consequence: Tax withheld falls from USD 39 to USD 19.50. Actual eligibility must be documented.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Position — market value used in the example; USD
Yield — annual gross dividend ÷ position value
Withholding — tax deducted from the distribution; %
Domicile — legal jurisdiction of the fund
Treaty eligibility — investor-specific entitlement requiring evidence
action: Complete an investor-to-fund implementation record with documented eligibility and source dates.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: The same underlying exposure can produce different outcomes through residence, domicile, withholding, custody and currency. Preserve the investor’s dated facts and document the entire route.

beats.title: Define jobs before tickers
points: A strategic core carries the enduring policy exposure.
A satellite takes a limited, explicit active risk.
Every sleeve needs a target, loss budget and decision authority.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Diversification depends on joint movement
points: Mixing equity and bonds changes both volatility and expected behaviour.
Portfolio standard deviation is not a weighted average of individual volatilities.
Correlation assumptions need a stress test when regimes change.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Architecture should constrain behaviour
points: Core-satellite, factor tilts and barbell designs make different commitments.
A concentrated sleeve needs a credible maximum-loss budget.
Choose a policy that the investor can fund, explain and maintain.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: Joint risk is not a weighted-average volatility
calculation.equation: σₚ² = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² + 2w₁w₂σ₁σ₂ρ
calculation.substitution: 70% equity / 30% bonds; 16% / 6% volatility; correlation 0.10 → portfolio σ 11.52%.
calculation.interpretation: The naive linear average is 13.00%; covariance explains the difference.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: A concentrated sleeve spends the loss budget
scenario.baseline: Teaching sleeve weight 10%; assumed loss 50%.
scenario.changed: Raise the sleeve weight to 20% with the same 50% loss.
scenario.consequence: Its portfolio loss contribution doubles from 5 to 10 percentage points, before other positions move.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: w — portfolio capital weight; decimal
σ — annualised standard deviation; decimal
ρ — correlation between the two return series
Variance — squared standard deviation
Loss budget — acceptable portfolio impact of the stress
action: Choose an architecture and write each sleeve’s purpose, target, loss budget and review authority.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: A portfolio architecture assigns jobs and limits to each sleeve. It becomes useful when risk budgets, funding and governance constrain later security choices.

beats.title: The benchmark comes before the ticker
points: SPYM provides S&P 500 exposure in the source comparison.
QQQM adds a deliberate Nasdaq-100 growth tilt.
A second fund may increase exposure to companies already held.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Look through the labels
points: Multiply fund weights by each underlying company weight.
Aggregate shared companies before assessing concentration.
Use HHI and effective holding count as diagnostics, not complete risk measures.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Contributions can repair drift
points: Send new cash to underweight sleeves before assuming a sale is needed.
Track spreads and liquidity alongside published fund fees.
Document the intended tilt and a maximum active weight.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: Concentration has an effective count
calculation.equation: HHI = Σwᵢ²; effective N = 1/HHI
calculation.substitution: 30 equal weights: HHI = 0.03333; effective N = 30.
calculation.interpretation: Unequal weights reduce the effective count even if the nominal holding count is unchanged.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: An equal nominal count can mask different concentration
scenario.baseline: Thirty equally weighted holdings have effective N of 30.
scenario.changed: Increase a few weights and reduce the rest while retaining 30 names.
scenario.consequence: HHI increases and effective N falls. Inspect common holdings across funds before interpreting the fund count.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: wᵢ — look-through weight of company i
HHI — sum of squared company weights
Effective N — 1/HHI; equally weighted equivalent count
Active weight — exposure above or below the benchmark
action: Document the core, intended tilt, look-through exposure and maximum active weight.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: A broad core and a growth fund can form a deliberate tilt rather than independent diversification. Look-through weights and a review rule make that intention visible.

beats.title: Semiconductors are a concentrated industry exposure
points: SOXQ, SOXX, SMH and XSD use different eligibility and weighting rules.
Foundry, design, equipment and memory businesses have different drivers.
A low expense ratio does not remove cyclical or geopolitical risk.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: The satellite overlaps the core
points: Aggregate company exposures across broad and thematic funds.
Weight concentration changes the impact of a single-company loss.
Test the semiconductor sleeve with growth and market exposures together.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Choose a loss budget before a theme
points: Size the sleeve using a plausible stress loss.
Set a target band and a thesis-break condition.
Record the evidence that would reduce, retain or exit the position.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: Size the satellite against a stress loss
calculation.equation: Portfolio loss contribution ≈ sleeve weight × sleeve loss
calculation.substitution: Illustration: 15% sleeve × −40% sleeve return = −6 percentage points.
calculation.interpretation: Other sleeves can fall at the same time. This isolates one contribution, not the full stress outcome.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Test the satellite without promising a loss limit
scenario.baseline: 15% satellite; illustrative −40% sleeve shock.
scenario.changed: Increase the weight to 20%, retaining the same shock.
scenario.consequence: Loss contribution rises from −6 to −8 percentage points; correlations can add wider portfolio losses.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Satellite weight — fraction of total portfolio capital
Stress return — assumed sleeve return in the scenario
Loss contribution — weight × stress return
Percentage point — additive impact on portfolio return
Thesis break — evidence that invalidates the sleeve rationale
action: Set a satellite target, band and thesis-break condition tied to named evidence.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: A thematic fund adds concentrated industry risk even when it holds multiple companies. Size the position against a portfolio loss budget and explicit thesis conditions.

beats.title: A premium pays for an obligation
points: A cash-secured put may require buying the underlying at the strike.
A covered call limits upside while retaining downside ownership risk.
The underlying must be suitable even if assignment occurs.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Contract size creates concentration
points: One standard contract represents 100 shares in the source example.
Cash collateral is committed capital, not freely available reserve.
A small premium cannot offset an arbitrarily large underlying loss.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Evaluate the complete cycle
points: Include premiums, underlying price change, costs and taxes.
Do not annualise one favourable cycle as an expected return.
Benchmark the strategy against a consistent underlying and cash alternative.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: The put premium does not remove downside
calculation.equation: Put payoff per share = premium − max(strike − ending price, 0)
calculation.substitution: Strike USD 90; premium USD 2; one contract → collateral USD 9,000 and premium USD 200.
calculation.interpretation: Assigned break-even is USD 88/share before fees and tax; the short put retains substantial downside.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Assignment can overwhelm the collected premium
scenario.baseline: The USD 90 put collects USD 2/share.
scenario.changed: The underlying ends at USD 70.
scenario.consequence: Payoff = 2 − (90 − 70) = USD −18/share, or USD −1,800 for one contract, before costs.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Strike — contracted exercise price; USD/share
Premium — cash received for the option; USD/share
Contract — 100 shares in this teaching example
Collateral — cash committed to the potential purchase
Payoff — result at expiration before fees and tax
action: Define eligible underlyings, collateral reserve and the response to a loss-and-assignment scenario.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: Option premium is compensation for an obligation. A tactical sleeve needs suitable underlying ownership, sufficient collateral and a complete downside-and-assignment plan.

beats.title: Integrate all sleeves into one policy
points: The illustrative allocation combines core equity, bonds, a growth tilt and a satellite.

Options collateral and cash reserves share the same balance sheet.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Risk contributions need a joint model
points: Volatility and correlations turn weights into portfolio variability.

Use scenario tables and review model assumptions before optimisation.

beats.title: Rebalancing is a rule, not a prediction

Document costs, taxes, liquidity and the person authorised to trade.

calculation.title: Calculate the trade from the current total
calculation.equation: Tradeᵢ = target weightᵢ × current portfolio value − current sleeve valueᵢ
calculation.substitution: Source SPYM: target USD 32,532.50 − current USD 31,625.00 = buy USD 907.50.
calculation.interpretation: The four source rebalance trades net to zero before transaction costs.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Use new contributions before assuming a sale

scenario.changed: Direct new cash toward underweight sleeves first.
scenario.consequence: Recalculate residual trades on the new portfolio total; compare taxes and costs before selling.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Target weight — policy allocation; decimal
Current value — marked sleeve value; USD
Target value — weight × total portfolio value; USD
Trade — target value less current value; USD
Drift — deviation of actual weight from the target
action: Adopt review dates, drift triggers and a contribution-first rule in one investment policy.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: Separate sleeves form one policy only when overlap, covariance, collateral, costs and rebalancing are considered together. A governance rule makes the portfolio maintainable.

beats.title: Funding has its own timing decision
points: Lump-sum investment and staged contributions expose cash at different dates.
Keep the total amount and comparison horizon consistent.
The useful choice depends on cash needs, risk capacity and implementation.

beats.title: Withdrawals make return order matter
points: The same set of annual returns can produce different ending balances.

Test reserves, flexible spending and rebalancing together.

beats.title: Maintenance is a household process
points: Revisit income, contributions, beneficiaries and near-term spending.
Separate documented policy changes from reactions to recent performance.
Preserve a review calendar and a decision record.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: Withdrawals change the sequence outcome
calculation.equation: Closing balance = opening balance × (1 + return) − withdrawal
calculation.substitution: USD 1m with bad years first ends at USD 666,446; the reordered path ends at USD 895,643.
calculation.interpretation: The source uses the same returns with USD 45,000 withdrawn annually at year end.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Return order matters after spending begins
scenario.baseline: Bad years first: ending wealth USD 666,446.24.
scenario.changed: Same returns reordered; bad years last: USD 895,643.36.
scenario.consequence: The difference is USD 229,197.12 under the source withdrawal schedule, despite the same set of returns.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Withdrawal — cash removed at the stated date; USD
Sequence risk — effect of return order with investor cash flows
Real wealth — nominal wealth adjusted for inflation
Reserve — accessible money for near-term spending
action: Add near-term spending, reserve sequencing and withdrawal review dates to the portfolio policy.
case: An educational US-market portfolio, funded and maintained through an explicit policy rather than a prediction of the next winning fund.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: Contribution and withdrawal timing connect investments to the household. Sequence tests, accessible reserves and scheduled reviews help keep the portfolio useful when life changes.

beats.title: Map the dependency, not the personality
points: List decisions, customer relationships and operating knowledge held by one person.
Identify which work stops if the founder is unavailable.
Prioritise dependencies by time to disruption and business consequence.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Authority and access need separate controls
points: A deputy needs authority to act, not merely a password.

Test handovers through real work with documented escalation.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

beats.title: Make continuity measurable
points: Build customer relationships beyond a single individual.
Use a short continuity plan with named deputies and contact routes.
Review performance through a ninety-day resilience programme.
beats.notes: Explain the mechanism with the cited article section, then relate it to the opening decision.

calculation.title: Make the response time visible
calculation.equation: Continuity gap = time to restore a critical function − tolerable interruption
calculation.substitution: Record each function’s tolerable interruption, deputy and tested recovery time.
calculation.interpretation: An untested deputy or inaccessible authorisation leaves a gap even if the plan looks complete.
calculation.notes: Article worked example and saved workbook evidence; preserve their separate assumptions.

scenario.title: Test an absence before it becomes a crisis
scenario.baseline: Founder approves payments, handles a key customer and holds critical knowledge.
scenario.changed: Run a planned absence with a named deputy and documented limits.
scenario.consequence: Record blocked decisions and delays; revise authority, training and customer ownership before repeating the test.
scenario.notes: Teaching sensitivity; hold other assumptions fixed unless a multi-input case is explicitly named.

units: Critical function — activity whose interruption causes material harm
Deputy — named person trained and authorised to act
Recovery time — tested time needed to resume the function
action: Create a dependency map, named deputies and a ninety-day programme of tested handovers.
case: A founder-led business rehearses who can serve customers, approve payments and recover critical records if the founder is unavailable.
caseLabel: Dated source record • fictional calculations are labelled as illustrations
answer: Key-person risk is concentration of knowledge, relationships and authority. Resilience improves when deputies perform real work and the continuity plan is tested.
